78.title: Eighty years
78.hook: his body like an old cart kept going with straps (DN 16)
78.howItsDone: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the account of the Buddha's last journey, is read and studied across Buddhist traditions, and many Buddhists reflect on aging, sickness and death as natural parts of life, as he did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nalagiri, the wild elephant, met with metta. Your line was the elephant kneels. Whose charge did you meet with a slow breath? Day seventy-eight, and a new week: the last days.

Think of an old car someone in your family refused to give up. The door that only opens from the inside. The duct tape on the mirror. It still gets there. Maybe you are that car some mornings. This week the path follows the Buddha's last journey, told in one long text, the Great Discourse on the Final Nibbana. It's one of the most human texts in the whole canon. He's around eighty now. He's still walking from town to town, still teaching. And during a rainy season near Vesali, he falls seriously ill, with sharp pains, close to death.
screen: `THE OLD CAR THAT STILL GETS THERE.` → `THE LAST JOURNEY.` → `EIGHTY, AND SERIOUSLY ILL.`

segments.voice: The text says he bore the pain mindfully, without complaint. And he thought: it wouldn't be right for me to pass away without speaking to those who attended me, without taking leave of the community. So, by strength of will, he pushed the illness back, and held on to life. When he's recovered enough, he comes out and sits in the shade. Ananda sits down beside him and admits how frightened he was. When I saw you sick, my body went weak, he says. I couldn't think straight. My only comfort was that you wouldn't go without leaving some instruction. And then the Buddha says something astonishingly frank about his own body. He says, in paraphrase: I'm old now, Ananda. Worn out. I've reached the end of my days. I'm turning eighty. And just as an old cart is kept going only by being held together with straps, the body of the one who has found the way is kept going only with that kind of help. A worn-out cart. That's how he describes himself. Not a glowing god. Not a body beyond aging. A man at eighty, held together with repairs. And he adds that his body is only comfortable when he rests his mind in deep meditation, beyond all the signs of things. Think about what this means for a moment. Buddhist tradition holds that he had reached complete freedom. And the body still aged. It still hurt. Awakening didn't stop the cart from wearing out. What it changed was how he rode it. And he kept rolling. The next pages have him still walking, still teaching, for months.
screen: `HE HOLDS ON, TO SAY GOODBYE.` · `ANANDA ADMITS HE WAS AFRAID.` · `LIKE AN OLD CART, HELD WITH STRAPS.` · `AWAKE, AND THE BODY STILL AGES.` · then, large: `THE OLD CART STILL ROLLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stretch gently and thank your body. Settle and breathe. Slowly roll your shoulders, once, twice. Tilt your head to one side, then the other. Stretch your fingers wide, and let them close. Whatever aches, notice it without scolding. Then, silently, thank this body, the whole worn, patched, faithful cart of it, for carrying you this far. It's still rolling. The bell holds the time.
Eighty years. The Buddha at the end of his life, describing his own body as an old cart kept going with straps.
Your line: the old cart still rolls. Today, when your body complains, answer it kindly instead of cursing it. It's been carrying you for years. Day seventy-eight.

what it means: the most human part: an old man, sick, frank about his body, still walking.

79.title: Be an island
79.hook: to Ananda: be islands to yourselves, a refuge to yourselves, the dhamma your refuge (DN 16)
79.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote 'be an island to yourself' (or 'be a lamp') to encourage self-reliance grounded in practice, and the four foundations of mindfulness that the Buddha names here are still taught as a meditation practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eighty years: the Buddha called his body an old cart held together with straps. Your line was the old cart still rolls. Did you thank yours? Day seventy-nine.

A waiting room, a phone that won't ring, and one question underneath everything: what happens to us without them? Ananda is sitting in the shade beside the Buddha, who has just come through a serious illness. Ananda has been his attendant for many years. And he admits that while the teacher lay sick, he held on to one comfort: surely the teacher would not pass away without leaving some last instruction for the community. Some plan. Someone in charge. The Buddha's answer is not the one Ananda was hoping for. It hands the question straight back to him.
screen: `WHAT HAPPENS WITHOUT THEM?` → `ANANDA WANTS A PLAN.` → `NOT THE ANSWER HE HOPED FOR.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha says, what does the community expect of me? I've taught everything, with nothing held back. There's no closed fist of a teacher here, no secret saved for the favorites. And I've never thought of myself as the one who must lead the community. So why would I leave a leader? Then comes the line. In Pali, the key word is dipa. And dipa has two meanings. It can mean an island, and it can mean a lamp. Translators have gone both ways. In 1881 T. W. Rhys Davids rendered it with lamps: "be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." Other translators hear island: be an island to yourself, a refuge to yourself, with the dhamma as your island, the dhamma as your refuge, and no other. Think about those two pictures. An island is solid ground when the flood is rising all around. A lamp is light when everyone else's has gone out. Either way, the point is the same. Don't lean your whole weight on a person, even me. Stand on what you've seen for yourself, and on the teaching itself. How? The Buddha answers right there. By practicing mindfulness: watching the body, feelings, the mind and the way things are, steadily, with clear attention. The island isn't stubbornness. It isn't going it alone. It's having practiced enough that when the waters rise, there's ground under your feet. A teacher who refuses to name a successor, and tells his students to be their own light, and their own ground.
screen: `NO CLOSED FIST, NOTHING HELD BACK.` · `DIPA: AN ISLAND, OR A LAMP.` · `THE DHAMMA AS YOUR REFUGE.` · `THE ISLAND IS BUILT BY PRACTICE.` · then, large: `BE YOUR OWN ISLAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide one thing yourself today. Settle and breathe. Feel the ground under you, the chair, the floor, the steadiness of it. That's your island for these two minutes. Now think of one small decision you've been waiting for someone else to make for you. What to eat. Whether to call. Which way to go. Ask yourself what you actually see, what you actually know. Let the answer come from your own ground. The bell holds the time.
Dipa. Island, and also lamp: the Buddha's answer to Ananda, be a dipa and a refuge to yourselves, with the dhamma your refuge.
Your line: be your own island. Today, make one decision from your own ground, without waiting for anyone's permission. Day seventy-nine.

80.title: Vesali is lovely
80.hook: he looks back at the city turning his whole body, like an elephant, and says how delightful it was (DN 16)
80.howItsDone: Pilgrims still visit Vaishali in Bihar, India, where an Ashokan pillar and stupa ruins mark places tied to the Buddha's life, and the 'elephant look' is remembered in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, read across Buddhist traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dipa: no successor, just the dhamma, and your own ground. Your line was be your own island. What did you decide yourself? Day eighty.

The last time you left a place you loved, did you look back? The apartment, emptied out, keys on the counter. A hometown in the rearview mirror. A hospital room. Some people can't help it. They turn around at the door. Vesali was a rich, lively city, full of shrines and gardens and a proud, independent people. The Buddha knew it well. It was where the women had walked to ask for ordination. Where a famous courtesan named Ambapali had given him a mango grove and a meal, beating the city's princes to the invitation. And in the last months of his life, the old texts show him in Vesali, enjoying it.
screen: `DID YOU LOOK BACK?` → `VESALI, A LIVELY CITY.` → `IN HIS LAST MONTHS, ENJOYING IT.`

segments.voice: The account has a quiet surprise here. One day, sitting at a shrine outside the city, the Buddha turns to Ananda and simply names the places he loves. Delightful is Vesali, Ananda. Delightful is this shrine, and that one, and that one, and he lists them by name. An awakened man, near the end of his life, enjoying the view. Some people imagine that letting go means not caring about anything. Being above it all. This moment says something else. He's free of clinging, and he can still say, this place is beautiful. Maybe that's exactly why he can say it so simply, without needing to keep it. Then comes the leaving. After his last alms round in Vesali, as he walks away, he stops and turns to look back at the city. The text says he looked back at Vesali with the elephant look. The commentary explains the phrase: an elephant doesn't glance over its shoulder; it turns its whole great body to look, and so did he. And he says to Ananda: this is the last time I will look at Vesali. That's all. No speech about impermanence, though he had taught it often. He just turns, fully, and looks. Then he turns back, and walks on. Two things held together, again. He loves it. He lets it go. Both, completely. Nothing half-turned. One full look at the city, and then the road to the next village.
screen: `DELIGHTFUL IS VESALI.` · `FREE OF CLINGING, STILL LOVING.` · `THE ELEPHANT LOOK.` · `THE LAST TIME I'LL SEE IT.` · then, large: `HOW LOVELY IT WAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back fondly at one place. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a place you loved and left. A childhood kitchen. A school. A city. A friend's porch. Walk through it slowly in your mind. See the light. Hear it. Then, the way an elephant turns, turn your whole attention toward it, and say quietly: how lovely it was. Let it be lovely. Then let it be past. The bell holds the time.
Nagapalokita. The elephant look: the Buddha turning his whole body toward Vesali, the places he loved, for one last look.
Your line: how lovely it was. Today, when you leave somewhere, turn fully around at the door and look once, before you go. Day eighty.

81.title: Cunda's meal
81.hook: the smith Cunda serves a last meal; the Buddha falls ill and makes sure Cunda is not blamed (DN 16)
81.howItsDone: Buddhists remember Cunda's meal as one of the two most blessed offerings of food, alongside Sujata's rice before the awakening, and the story is often told to show the Buddha's care for others' feelings even in his final illness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nagapalokita, the elephant look: one full turn toward a city he loved. Your line was how lovely it was. Where did you look back? Day eighty-one.

A cook stays up all night over one meal for a guest he admires. In the morning the guest sits down and eats. That night the guest falls terribly ill. It is hard to think of a heavier thing for a cook to carry. In the town of Pava, a metalworker named Cunda hears that the Buddha is staying in his mango grove. Cunda goes, listens to him teach, and invites him and the monks to a meal at his home the next day. He spends the night preparing good food. In the morning the Buddha comes, and sits, and eats. And that meal turns out to be his last.
screen: `COOKING FOR SOMEONE YOU ADMIRE.` → `CUNDA THE SMITH, IN PAVA.` → `THE LAST MEAL.`

segments.voice: Among the dishes is one called sukaramaddava. And here we have to say plainly: nobody knows exactly what it was. Its parts mean pig and soft, or tender, and even that doesn't settle it. Some ancient commentators said it was tender pork. Others said it was a kind of mushroom or truffle, the sort pigs root for. Others said bamboo shoots, or a special preparation. Buddhists and scholars still argue about it, and the text leaves it open. What the text does record is strange and careful. The Buddha tells Cunda: serve that dish only to me. Give the others the rest of the food. And whatever is left of it, bury in a pit. I see no one in the world who could digest it but me. Cunda does as he's told. After the meal, a severe illness comes on, with bleeding and sharp pains. The Buddha bears it, mindful and calm, and keeps walking toward Kusinara. And then, on the road, he thinks of Cunda. He tells Ananda: someone may make Cunda feel guilty. They'll say, it's your loss, friend Cunda, that the Buddha died after eating your food. If that happens, go to him. Tell him that two meals are equal in blessing, greater than all others. The meal the Buddha ate just before his awakening, and the meal he ate just before his final passing. Cunda's gift is one of those two. In pain, near the end, the Buddha's mind turns to a man who might blame himself, and he arranges comfort for him in advance. Not a word about fault. Only: this was a great gift.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT THE DISH WAS.` · `SERVE IT ONLY TO ME.` · `A SEVERE ILLNESS, BORNE CALMLY.` · `TWO MEALS EQUAL IN BLESSING.` · then, large: `NO ONE IS TO BLAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect someone from blame. Settle and breathe. Think of someone who might be blaming themselves for something that went wrong. A friend whose plan fell through. A coworker who made an honest mistake. A parent. Maybe it's you. Picture them, and notice the weight they're carrying. Then think of one thing you could say, the way the Buddha sent word to Cunda, that would lift a little of it. The bell holds the time.
Cunda's meal. The last meal, offered by a smith in Pava. The Buddha fell ill, and made sure Cunda would never be blamed.
Your line: no one is to blame. Today, when something goes wrong, look for the person who's blaming themselves, and tell them what they gave. Day eighty-one.

82.title: Between two sal trees
82.hook: at Kusinara he lies down on his right side; the trees blossom out of season (DN 16)
82.carry: rest is part of the path
82.howItsDone: Reclining Buddha images, showing him on his right side between the sal trees at Kusinara, are found in temples across Asia, and pilgrims visit Kushinagar in India, where a large reclining image marks the place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cunda's meal, and a dying teacher who made sure the cook was never blamed. Your line was no one is to blame. Whose weight did you lift? Day eighty-two.

If you've ever visited a Buddhist temple, you may have seen him lying down. A huge golden figure, stretched out on his right side, head resting on one hand, eyes half closed, calm as a Sunday afternoon. It's easy to take it for a nap. It's something else. It's today. After Cunda's meal, sick and weak, the Buddha walks on toward a small town called Kusinara. He stops to rest along the way. He crosses a river. And at a grove of sal trees outside the town, he says to Ananda: I'm tired. I want to lie down.
screen: `THE RECLINING BUDDHA.` → `NOT A NAP.` → `I'M TIRED. I WANT TO LIE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Please, Ananda, he says, prepare a couch for me between these two sal trees, with my head to the north. Ananda does. And the Buddha lies down on his right side, in what's called the lion's posture, one foot resting on the other, mindful and clearly aware. That's the pose in the great statues. Not sleep. Awake, at rest, at the end. Then the text says the twin sal trees burst into flower, out of season, and blossoms drift down onto his body. Flowers and sandalwood powder fall from the sky, and music plays from somewhere above, all in his honor. And here's the turn. The Buddha says to Ananda, in effect: this is not how the one who found the way is truly honored. Not with flowers. Whoever lives by the teaching, practicing it well, in small matters and great, that person honors him. Even with the trees in bloom, he points away from the show and back to the practice. And there's something quietly radical about the simplest part. He lay down. The great teacher, who had walked from town to town all his teaching life, said he was tired, and rested. The path wasn't only effort. Rest was part of it, especially here. In the same hours, the text tells of Ananda going off alone, leaning on a doorpost, and weeping. My teacher is passing away, he says, the one who was so kind to me. The Buddha sends for him, and comforts him, and praises him in front of everyone. Tomorrow, one more visitor arrives at the grove.
screen: `HEAD TO THE NORTH, ON HIS RIGHT SIDE.` · `SAL TREES BLOOM OUT OF SEASON.` · `HONOR ME BY PRACTICE.` · `ANANDA WEEPS BY THE DOOR.` · then, large: `REST IS PART OF THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lie down for one mindful minute, or two. If you can, lie down now, on your right side if that's comfortable, or on your back. If you can't, lean back and let your body be heavy. Feel what holds you up. Feel your breath slow down by itself. There's nothing to do and nowhere to get to. Rest, awake. Let this be practice too. The bell holds the time.
Between two sal trees. The grove at Kusinara where the Buddha lay down on his right side, awake and at rest, as the trees bloomed out of season.
Your line: rest is part of the path. Today, when you're tired, say so, and rest for a few minutes without apologizing. Day eighty-two.

83.title: The last disciple
83.hook: the wanderer Subhadda is turned away at the door; the Buddha calls him in (DN 16)
83.howItsDone: Buddhists remember Subhadda as the last disciple the Buddha personally taught, and the story is often told to show that the door to the teaching stays open to anyone who asks sincerely.

segments.voice: Yesterday, between two sal trees, the Buddha lay down, awake, and the trees bloomed. Your line was rest is part of the path. Did you let yourself rest? Day eighty-three.

You know the feeling of arriving just as the doors are closing. The store's locking up. Visiting hours ended five minutes ago. Someone behind the glass shakes their head. Sorry. Too late. In Kusinara that night, word goes around: the teacher Gotama will pass away in the last watch of the night. A wandering seeker named Subhadda hears it. He's not a follower. He belongs to another group of wanderers. But he has a question that's been nagging at him for years, and he thinks: this teacher might be the one who can clear it up. It's now or never. So he hurries out to the sal grove, in the dark.
screen: `JUST AS THE DOORS CLOSE.` → `A WANDERER WITH A QUESTION.` → `NOW OR NEVER.`

segments.voice: At the edge of the grove, Subhadda meets Ananda and asks: may I see the teacher? And Ananda, loyal, exhausted, grieving, says: enough, friend Subhadda. Don't trouble him. He's weary. Subhadda asks again. Ananda says no again. A third time. No. You can understand Ananda completely. He's protecting someone he loves in his last hours. But the Buddha, lying between the trees, hears them. And he says: enough, Ananda. Don't keep Subhadda out. Let him come. Whatever he asks, he'll ask because he wants to understand, not to bother me. So Subhadda comes in and sits, and asks his question. There are all these famous teachers, heads of big schools, and each says he's found the truth. Have they all really understood? Or none of them? Or some? And the Buddha waves the comparison away. Let that be, Subhadda. Never mind them. I'll teach you the thing itself. And he tells him simply: wherever the noble eightfold path is found, there you'll find people who truly practice it and reach its fruits. Subhadda asks to go forth, right there. The Buddha asks Ananda to ordain him. And the text says that, living earnestly, not long after, Subhadda reached the goal. He was the last person the Buddha taught directly. Notice who got in. Not a longtime monk. An outsider, from another group, arriving after hours with a question. And the dying teacher overrode his own protective attendant to make room. The door wasn't closed yet. There was still time.
screen: `ENOUGH, DON'T TROUBLE HIM.` · `LET HIM COME.` · `NEVER MIND THE OTHERS.` · `THE LAST ONE HE TAUGHT.` · then, large: `THERE'S STILL TIME.`

segments.voice: Settle and breathe, and make room for one late arrival. Think of someone who shows up late in your life. The friend who always texts after the plans are set. The person who joined the team last. A question you keep putting off because it came at a bad time. Picture the door, and your hand on it, about to close. Then open it a little wider. There's room. The bell holds the time.
Subhadda. The wanderer turned away three times at the door, and called in by the dying Buddha himself, the last disciple he taught.
Your line: there's still time. Today, say yes to one person who asks at an inconvenient moment. Day eighty-three.

84.title: The last words
84.hook: "decay is inherent in all component things; work out your salvation with diligence" (DN 16, Rhys Davids)
84.howItsDone: In Theravada countries Vesak remembers the parinibbana together with the birth and awakening, East Asian traditions keep Nirvana Day, and the last words on heedfulness are often recited and quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subhadda, turned away three times, called in by the Buddha. Your line was there's still time. Who did you make room for? Day eighty-four.

What would you say, if you knew they were your last words? Some famous last words are funny, some are grand, and some were polished by whoever wrote them down. It's deep in the night now at Kusinara, between the sal trees. The monks are gathered around. Ananda is there. Subhadda has been ordained. And the Buddha has a few things left to say. First, practical things. When I'm gone, he tells Ananda, don't think you have no teacher. The teaching and the discipline I've given you will be your teacher. Then he asks the monks, three times, if anyone has any doubt left about the teaching. Ask now, so you won't regret it. Nobody speaks.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOUR LAST WORDS BE?` → `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.` → `ANY DOUBT? ASK NOW.`

segments.voice: Then come the last words. In the 1881 translation by T. W. Rhys Davids, the Buddha says to the monks: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Everything put together comes apart. So keep going, with care. The Pali word at the heart of it is appamada, which means something like heedfulness, carefulness, not letting yourself drift. A modern rendering puts it: strive on with diligence. That's it. Not a dramatic promise. Not a claim about himself. The same two things he had taught all along, compressed into one breath: things end, so practice. Then he passes through the stages of deep meditation, up and back down and up again, and from the fourth, the text says, he passes away. Today's word is the name for that: parinibbana, complete nibbana, the full going-out of an awakened one at death. Buddhist traditions understand that ending in more than one way, and the Buddha himself refused to describe it in ordinary terms of existing or not existing. The earth trembles. Ananda speaks a short, shaken verse. In Theravada countries, the festival of Vesak remembers this night together with the birth and the awakening, on one full-moon day. Now look back at this week, the last days. The old cart that still rolled. Be your own island. Vesali, lovely, and the elephant look. Cunda's meal, and no one to blame. Rest between two sal trees. Subhadda, and still time. And today, the last words. The whole life, in the end, comes down to a line you could carry in your pocket.

Parinibbana. Complete nibbana: the final passing of an awakened one, at Kusinara, after the last words.
Your line: strive on with care. Today, when you notice yourself drifting, come back to what matters, gently, without scolding. Day eighty-four.
